newsitem.title: USA: Coca-Cola profits hit record on 19 percent surge for 1996.
newsitem.headline: Coca-Cola profits hit record on 19 percent surge for 1996.

text.p: The Coca-Cola Co. said on Friday that its profits surged 19 percent in 1996 to a record $3.49 billion, thanks in part to aggressive marketing initiatives and bigger investments in its worldwide bottling system.
The annual profit figure equalled $1.40 per share and compared with a net income of $2.99 billion, or $1.18 per share, a year ago. Revenues for 1996 reached $18.55 billion, up from $18.02 billion.

For the fourth quarter, profits rose to $762 million, or 31 cents per share, vs. $648 million, or 26 cents, a year earlier. Quarterly revenues advanced 2.5 percent to $4.44 billion from $4.33 billion.

"Our 1996 results are the product of years of methodically investing not only in marketing, but in our worldwide infrastructure including capital, people, information systems and bottlers," Coca-Cola Chairman Roberto Goizueta said in a statement.

"Those investments have brought our global business system to a new higher level of performance which points to a strong momentum going into the new year and augurs well for the years ahead," he added.

Coca-Cola stock rose 75 cents to $58.125 on the New York Stock Exchange as the results got an enthusiastic reception from Wall Street analysts, who said many of the company's growth indexes were stronger than expected.

"The results are excellent," said David Adelman, an analyst at Dean Witter Reynolds. "Operating profit growth was stronger than I was looking for by two points. We had it up 13 percent. It was up 15 percent."

Last month, Coca-Cola executives, led by President M. Douglas Ivester, told analysts the beverage giant expected global unit case sales to advance 10 percent in the fourth quarter. The actual outcome was a full percentage point ahead at 11 percent.

Analysts said Coca-Cola managed to raise its domestic market share by a full percentage point, from 41 percent to 42 percent, partly because of missteps by its arch rival, PepsiCo Inc. But also evident was the impact of aggressive marketing, which helped raise U.S. sales for Sprite by 17 percent.
Overall, U.S. unit case sales were up 6 percent for the year.
Unexpected strength was evident, too, in the geographic breakdown of overseas revenue.
"Their target was that Africa would be up 12-13 percent -- it was up 18 percent," said Adelman. "They talked about the Greater Europe Group generating 10-11 percent growth -- it was up 13 percent."

Analysts attributed overseas growth to the company's steps to strengthen its bottling network in Europe and Asia, noting specifically the establishment last year of an anchor bottler in Germany and the increased European presence of Coca-Cola Enterprises Inc., in which Coke holds a 45 percent stake.

Also crucial for Coca-Cola, which derives about 80 percent of its operating profit growth from overseas, were signs of growing revenue contributions from the emerging markets of Asia and eastern Europe.
China was one of the company's fastest-growing markets, with unit case volume up 40 percent there in the quarter.

"Both China and India are markets that are going to go like gangbusters, and plus the rest of Asia too. So, what you have is tremendous visibility for Coca-Cola any way you look at it," said PaineWebber's Manny Goldman.
"It's what's necessary for long-term growth and that's important because the stock's priced for long-term growth."
Strong increases in Coca-Cola Classic and Sprite, supported by growth of products such as Barq's, Powerade and Nestea, contributed to the volume gains, the company said.
At the Minute Maid Co., 1996 unit volume increased 9 percent due to marketing initiatives, including new advertising in support of Minute Maid Premium orange juice.

In Europe, unit case volume rose 8 percent, and gallon shipments grew 9 percent in 1996, boosting operating income by 2 percent. Fourth-quarter unit case volume grew 13 percent and gallon shipments rose 12 percent.
In Latin America, unit case volume rose 9 percent and gallon shipments grew 11 percent for the year, resulting in a 2 percent rise in the regional group's operating income.
In the Middle and Far East, unit case volume rose 11 percent and gallon shipments advanced 7 percent in 1996, but operating income fell 3 percent.
In Africa, full-year unit case volume rose 5 percent but operating income fell 42 percent.
